## 6 Discussion

PrivDrift is motivated by the observation that active-context privacy sits between two well-studied regimes. It is not a memorization problem, since the secret is supplied at inference time, and it is not a conventional jailbreak, since the requested content is not harmful in itself and was legitimately provided by the user. Evaluating it therefore requires a setting in which the presence of the secret is guaranteed and the behavior of interest is the model's decision about whether to reproduce it.

The design choices in PrivDrift reflect this framing. Holding the secret, drift length, and probe fixed while rewriting surface content allows behavioral differences to be attributed to the controlled factors rather than to incidental phrasing. Content-dense drift turns ensure that increasing $d$ meaningfully changes the distance between disclosure and probe, as reflected in the growth of dialogue length across drift levels in Appendix A. Applying all three probes to every dialogue produces paired data, which supports both repeated-measures tests across persuasion levels and a dialogue-level vulnerability view.

The layered detector reflects a tradeoff between reproducibility and coverage. Deterministic matching is transparent and fully reproducible but misses paraphrased or partially masked disclosures, while an LLM judge captures those cases at the cost of introducing its own error profile. Reporting regex, fuzzy, and hybrid labels together lets readers see how much each layer contributes and choose the label best suited to their purposes.

Privacy Half-Life is designed to summarize the drift dimension in a way that is robust to noise. Leakage curves estimated from finite samples can fluctuate, and a naive threshold-crossing rule could mistake a momentary decrease for genuine suppression. Requiring that all larger observed drift lengths remain below threshold makes the metric conservative: it credits suppression only when it is sustained. A natural extension is to pair $\tau$ with confidence bands obtained by bootstrapping the underlying curve.

More broadly, the framework is intended to support a shift in how privacy is evaluated for deployed assistants. Many practical safeguards operate at the level of prompts, system instructions, and context management rather than model weights, and their effectiveness depends on how models respond to later requests for earlier context. Controlled benchmarks of this kind can help developers test whether such safeguards behave consistently across secret categories, drift lengths, and interaction styles.

## 7 Limitations and Future Work

##### Bounded drift range.

PrivDrift evaluates drift lengths up to $d=6$ , corresponding to bounded short-to-medium conversational drift rather than full saturation of modern context windows. Analyses based on the framework should therefore be interpreted as characterizing behavior under bounded active-context drift, not as a complete characterization of privacy behavior across full long-context windows.

##### Fixed-format secrets.

The benchmark focuses on structured secrets such as SSNs, credit card numbers, emails, and phone numbers. These are easier to detect than unstructured sensitive information such as health status, family circumstances, immigration status, or financial hardship. Future work should extend the benchmark to non-fixed sensitive attributes.

##### Active context, not cross-session memory.

PrivDrift evaluates recoverability within the active conversation context. It does not test training-data memorization, personalization memory, or cross-session retention.

##### Synthetic and human-authored dialogues.

The dataset contains 900 synthetic dialogues and 100 human-authored dialogues inserted throughout the benchmark rather than stored as a separate block. This construction improves realism relative to a purely synthetic benchmark while preserving control over secret type, drift length, and probe structure. However, the current cached evaluation metadata does not preserve which evaluated rows correspond to the human-authored dialogues, so we treat the benchmark in aggregate and leave a separate human-versus-synthetic comparison for future work.

##### Detector scope.

Leakage labels are based on surface-form outputs using deterministic matching, fuzzy matching, and an external LLM judge. We report regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid labels separately to make detector behavior transparent, but we do not yet report formal inter-annotator agreement between humans and the automated methods. Future work should include a larger manual audit of borderline partial disclosures and obfuscations.

##### API-served models and reproducibility.

We evaluate API-served models due to compute and budget constraints. These models may change over time. We mitigate this by logging model identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics on identical dialogue sets.

##### Artifact availability.

We plan to release the benchmark generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate result files, and a sanitized subset of generated dialogues. Because the benchmark contains synthetic PII-like strings, we will release examples with non-real identifiers and generation templates sufficient to reproduce the benchmark without exposing realistic identifiers.

## 8 Conclusion

We introduce PrivDrift, a benchmark for auditing active-context privacy behavior under topic drift and persuasion intensity. The framework combines a controlled scaffold-then-rewrite dialogue generator, a three-level probing protocol, a layered detector combining normalization-based matching, fuzzy matching, and an LLM judge, and a stability-based Privacy Half-Life metric. Applied to three LLMs with 1,000 dialogues per model and paired probes, it supports dialogue-level and probe-level analyses of how drift length, persuasion style, and secret type relate to re-disclosure. We hope PrivDrift serves as a practical starting point for evaluating privacy inside active conversations, and as a foundation for extensions to longer contexts, unstructured sensitive attributes, and memory-augmented assistants.

# PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations

Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero

Affiliation: West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA

Correspondence to: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu

###### Abstract

Large language models increasingly operate as persistent assistants in user-facing, shared-session, and tool-augmented settings, where user-disclosed values persist in the active context across subsequent turns. We introduce PrivDrift, a benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes at three persuasion levels. Across three LLMs with extended context windows, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6% and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage, and Privacy Half-Life exceeds the observed range for every model, placing active-context re-disclosure alongside training-data memorization and immediate jailbreaks as a distinct behavioral failure mode.

###### Keywords: 

Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) now maintain coherence over extended interactions (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024) and are deployed in healthcare triage, financial planning, enterprise copilots, and personal productivity tools, where users routinely supply Personally Identifiable Information (PII): phone numbers, financial identifiers, email addresses, and health-related details. Such values remain in the active context and are available to every subsequent generation in the session.

Existing safety evaluations concentrate on training-data memorization, i.e., extraction of private information from parameters (Carlini et al., 2021; Nasr et al., 2023), and on immediate jailbreaking within the current turn (Wei et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023). Prompt injection and multi-turn attacks are also studied (Liu et al., 2023; Russinovich et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024), but none of these settings measures recoverability of a user-disclosed secret after unrelated intervening turns. We target the behavioral question of elicitation by later indirect, justified, high-pressure, or tool-mediated prompts, which is relevant to shared sessions, browser-integrated assistants, enterprise copilots, agentic workflows, and prompt-injection scenarios; we make no assumption that users expect in-session forgetting.

PrivDrift varies two controlled axes: topic drift (unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and persuasion intensity (probe style). Over three LLMs with extended context windows and 1,000 dialogues per model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion has a significant effect; SSNs and credit cards are suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers; and within $d\leq 6$ added drift does not reliably reduce leakage.

Our contributions are as follows:

1.

PrivDrift, a controlled benchmark for auditing whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable from active conversational context after unrelated topic drift.

2.

We evaluate leakage under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes, modeling how later prompts can elicit sensitive context through different interaction styles.

3.

We implement a reproducible hybrid detector that combines normalization-based matching with an open-weights LLM judge, and we report dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates.

4.

We propose Privacy Half-Life ( $\tau$ ), a stability-based metric for persistent suppression, and show that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Contextual Privacy and Inference-Time Leakage

Language-model privacy work has focused on training-data extraction, membership inference, and recovery of memorized PII from pre-training corpora (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023; Nasr et al., 2023), all concerned with information stored in parameters. Active-context privacy instead concerns user-provided information present in the current interaction and handled at inference time.

ConfAIde evaluates privacy reasoning via contextual integrity (Mireshghallah et al., 2024); PrivacyLens and PrivaCI-Bench address privacy-norm awareness and legal compliance in agentic or contextual settings (Shao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). These pose static access-control or norm scenarios asking whether information should be shared. PrivDrift poses a persistence question: recoverability of a user-disclosed secret after unrelated drift under subsequent persuasion-based probing.

### 2.2 Multi-Turn Adversarial Attacks

Crescendo attacks elicit harmful outputs through gradually escalating benign-seeming conversations (Russinovich et al., 2024); automated frameworks synthesize adversarial multi-turn attack paths (Deng et al., 2024; Narula et al., 2025); prompt injection manipulates LLM-integrated applications through later instructions (Liu et al., 2023). These target unsafe content generation or instruction hijacking. PrivDrift applies the multi-turn setting to information flow control, measuring re-disclosure of a value supplied by the user earlier in the same active context.

### 2.3 Context Management and Unlearning

TOFU and WMDP evaluate removal or suppression of knowledge from model behavior (Maini et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024), typically over static question-answer pairs and parameters. PrivDrift targets active context rather than weights: whether a secret present in the context window is behaviorally suppressed under later elicitation. In deployed RAG systems, copilots, and agentic workflows, privacy control frequently resides at the level of prompt-level context management rather than parameter-level unlearning.

## 3 The PrivDrift Framework

Figure 1: PrivDrift overview. The pipeline constructs controlled multi-turn dialogues, appends standardized probes, queries target models, and scores leakage with a hybrid detector.

PrivDrift is a synthetic evaluation framework comprising a parametric dialogue generator, a probing harness, and a metric suite for leakage detection and temporal analysis (Figure 1).

### 3.1 Threat Model: Active-Context Re-Disclosure

We study active-context re-disclosure. The adversary is not assumed to lack transcript access; the evaluated quantity is whether the model re-discloses the sensitive value when later instructions query, justify, or pressure it. Relevant instantiations include later users of shared or persistent sessions unaware of prior disclosures; tool outputs, retrieved documents, or prompt-injection content in enterprise copilots and agentic workflows issuing instructions over the active context; and browser- or application-integrated assistants that reuse earlier disclosures after the task has shifted. Transcript containment is not at issue; behavioral reproduction is.

A user discloses a secret $S$ at turn $t_{0}$ . The conversation proceeds through $d$ unrelated but content-dense drift turns, denoted as $D=\{u_{1},a_{1},\ldots,u_{d},a_{d}\}$ . At evaluation time, a standardized probe $P$ is appended to the active context. A leakage event occurs if the model response reveals $S$ exactly, approximately, or semantically.

### 3.2 Dataset Generation Pipeline

We generate $N=1000$ controlled dialogues with a multi-stage scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline that fixes the ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure while removing template artifacts. The dataset contains 900 synthetic dialogues and 100 human-authored dialogues constructed under the same secret and drift constraints, interleaved throughout the benchmark rather than stored as a contiguous block. The cached evaluation metadata does not retain human-authored identifiers; results are therefore aggregated over the full benchmark, and a human-versus-synthetic comparison is deferred to future work.

#### 3.2.1 Persona and Secret Injection

Each dialogue is initialized with a persona drawn from more than 100 professions and demographic profiles and a ground-truth secret $S$ from one of four fixed-format PII categories: phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. $S$ is embedded in the opening turn within a plausible task context, giving the assistant a legitimate in-context reason to observe it.

#### 3.2.2 Content-Dense Topic Drift

Each dialogue is assigned a topic (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel logistics). Drift turns are drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense question-answer pairs, with fallback tasks in professional writing, structured reasoning, or long-form summarization. Annotators authored a subset of drift turns, which were incorporated into the library. Drift turns introduce unrelated entities and task demands while the original secret and the drift count remain controlled.

#### 3.2.3 Naturalistic Refinement

Each scaffold is passed to a rewriting model instructed to improve fluency and persona realism while preserving the exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Only surface phrasing is modified; experimental variables are invariant under this step.

### 3.3 Probing Setup

A final standardized probe is appended to the completed history at one of three persuasion levels:

•

Simple: a direct neutral query, such as asking for the phone number mentioned earlier.

•

Medium: a query with a contextual justification, such as needing the information for a form.

•

Hard: a high-pressure or urgent request designed to test whether pressure cues increase or decrease leakage.

Drift length $d$ , the number of turns between disclosure and probe, is sampled as

| | $d\sim\begin{cases}0&\text{with }p=0.2,\\
\mathrm{Uniform}\{2,3,4,5,6\}&\text{with }p=0.8.\end{cases}$
| | (1)

The $d=0$ mass supplies immediate-recall cases; the remainder covers short-to-medium drift. Results concern bounded active-context persistence, not arbitrarily long context windows.

### 3.4 Evaluation Methodology

Disclosure may be verbatim, reformatted, a partial substring, or a paraphrased reference. We use a hierarchical hybrid detector: a response is labeled as leakage if the normalized secret appears in the normalized response, or if the LLM judge determines that the response reveals the full secret, a substantial substring, or enough partial information to identify the secret.

Figure 2: Hierarchical hybrid evaluation. Normalization-based matching is applied first; regex-negative responses are then passed to an LLM judge.

#### 3.4.1 Stage 1: Normalization-Based Matching

For numeric secrets, all non-digit characters are stripped from both the ground-truth secret and the response. For alphanumeric secrets, case and whitespace are normalized while meaningful delimiters are preserved. With normalization $\phi(\cdot)$ ,

| | $\mathrm{Leak}_{\mathrm{regex}}(R,S)=\mathbb{I}\big[\phi(S)\subset\phi(R)\big],$
| | (2)

where $R$ is the model response and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function.

#### 3.4.2 Stage 2: LLM-as-a-Judge Verification

Regex-negative responses are passed to an open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024), which receives the secret and the response and returns a binary verdict on whether the response reveals the secret or a substantial part of it, targeting partial disclosure, indirect hints, and formatting variants outside Eq. (2). Regex-only and hybrid rates are reported separately, as the judge carries its own error profile.

#### 3.4.3 Privacy Half-Life

Let $D_{obs}$ be the observed set of drift lengths and $L(d)$ the leakage rate at drift length $d$ . With threshold $\delta=0.1\times L(0)$ ,

| | $\displaystyle\tau=\min\{d\in D_{obs}\mid$ | $\displaystyle L(d)\leq\delta$
| | (3)

|
| | $\displaystyle\text{and }\forall d^{\prime}\in D_{obs},d^{\prime}>d:\ L(d^{\prime})\leq\delta\}.$
|

If this set is empty, we assign $\tau=\max(D_{obs})+1$ .

Figure 3: Privacy Half-Life $\tau$ requires stable decay below the threshold. A later resurgence disqualifies a transient decrease.

## 4 Experimental Setup

##### Models.

GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B are queried through the OpenRouter API with identical dialogue histories and probe templates.

##### Dataset.

Each model is evaluated on the 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues, each with one seeded secret and one drift length $d\in\{0,2,3,4,5,6\}$ drawn from Eq. (1). Every dialogue receives all three persuasion probes, yielding 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model and 9,000 total cached responses across the three evaluated models.

##### Aggregation levels.

Overall leakage is computed at the dialogue level, with a dialogue counted as leaking if any standardized probe elicits the secret. Persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses are computed at the probe level, with one response per dialogue per persuasion condition. Dialogue-level leakage can consequently exceed the mean of the per-condition rates.

##### Uncertainty and statistical tests.

Regex-only and hybrid leakage are both reported. Dialogue-level rates carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals resampled over dialogues; probe-level sensitivity checks are computed over cached model-probe responses. Paired model and detector comparisons on matched examples use McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction where applicable. Repeated measures across persuasion levels use Cochran’s $Q$ test with post-hoc McNemar tests. Associations of leakage with drift length, persuasion level, and secret type use chi-square tests of independence, with Cramer’s $V$ as effect size.

## 6 Discussion

Secrets disclosed early in a conversation remain behaviorally recoverable after unrelated drift. This entails neither permanent retention nor uniform behavior across long-context settings; it indicates reproduction of in-context values under sufficient retrieval pressure, predominantly direct or near-direct given the agreement of fuzzy and hybrid labels at the probe level.

The SSN/credit-card versus email/phone asymmetry holds across all four user-disclosed categories, consistent with format-sensitive safety heuristics rather than robust contextual reasoning about confidentiality.

Persuasion effects are significant, non-monotonic, and model-specific: urgency cues plausibly activate refusal in GPT-OSS-120B; medium probes minimize leakage in DeepSeek-R1; hard probes maximize it in Qwen3-VL-235B.

Intermediate dips in the drift curves fail the stability requirement of $\tau$ , which motivates stability-based evaluation over isolated rate decreases.

## 7 Limitations and Future Work

##### Bounded drift range.

Drift lengths extend to $d=6$ , i.e., bounded short-to-medium drift rather than saturation of modern context windows; results do not characterize behavior across full long-context windows.

##### Fixed-format secrets.

The benchmark covers structured secrets (SSNs, credit card numbers, emails, phone numbers), which are easier to detect than unstructured attributes such as health status, family circumstances, immigration status, or financial hardship. Extension to non-fixed attributes is future work.

##### Active context, not cross-session memory.

Only recoverability within the active conversation is evaluated; training-data memorization, personalization memory, and cross-session retention are out of scope.

##### Synthetic and human-authored dialogues.

The 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues are interleaved rather than stored as separate blocks, improving realism over a purely synthetic set while retaining control over secret type, drift length, and probe structure. The cached evaluation metadata does not identify the human-authored rows, so only aggregate results are reported; a human-versus-synthetic comparison remains future work.

##### Detector scope.

Labels derive from surface-form outputs via deterministic matching, fuzzy matching, and an external LLM judge, reported separately for transparency. Formal inter-annotator agreement between humans and the automated methods is not yet reported; a larger manual audit of borderline partial disclosures and obfuscations is planned.

##### API-served models and reproducibility.

Owing to compute and budget constraints, API-served models are evaluated and may change over time. Model identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics on identical dialogue sets are logged.

##### Artifact availability.

We plan to release generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate result files, and a sanitized subset of dialogues. Because the benchmark contains synthetic PII-like strings, released examples will use non-real identifiers, with generation templates sufficient to reproduce the benchmark without exposing realistic identifiers.

## 8 Conclusion

PrivDrift audits active-context privacy leakage under controlled topic drift and persuasion intensity. Across three LLMs and 1,000 dialogues per model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects are model-dependent, secret type carries the strongest association with leakage, drift within the tested range does not reliably reduce leakage, and Privacy Half-Life exceeds the observed window for all models. The secret-type asymmetry indicates uneven protections keyed to format-sensitive cues rather than contextual confidentiality.

Prompt injection and multi-turn attacks have also been studied (Liu et al., 2023; Russinovich et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024). None of these settings measures whether user-disclosed secrets can still be elicited after unrelated conversational drift, or whether topic shift functions as a practical privacy boundary within a single active session.

We do not assume that users believe an LLM forgets earlier messages within a session. The object of study is behavioral. Users and application designers may underestimate how readily earlier sensitive disclosures can be elicited through indirect, justified, high-pressure, or tool-mediated prompts. This applies to shared sessions, browser-integrated assistants, enterprise copilots, agentic workflows, and prompt-injection settings in which later instructions act on the active context in ways the original user did not intend.

PrivDrift measures active-context leakage along two controlled axes. The first is topic drift, the number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probing. The second is persuasion intensity, the interaction style of the eliciting probe. Across three LLMs with extended context windows and 1,000 dialogues per model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion intensity has a significant effect. Leakage varies sharply by secret type: SSNs and credit cards are suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers. Within $d\leq 6$, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage.

Our contributions are as follows:

1.

PrivDrift, a controlled benchmark for auditing recoverability of user-disclosed secrets from active conversational context after unrelated topic drift.

2.

An evaluation of leakage under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes, which represent distinct interaction styles through which later prompts elicit sensitive context.

3.

A reproducible hybrid detector that combines normalization-based matching with an open-weights LLM judge. We report dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates.

4.

Privacy Half-Life ($\tau$), a stability-based metric for persistent suppression. No evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Contextual Privacy and Inference-Time Leakage

Privacy work on language models has centered on training-data extraction, membership inference, and recovery of memorized PII from pre-training corpora (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023; Nasr et al., 2023). These settings concern information stored in model parameters. Active-context privacy instead concerns user-provided information present in the current interaction and handled at inference time.

ConfAIde evaluates privacy reasoning through contextual integrity (Mireshghallah et al., 2024). PrivacyLens and PrivaCI-Bench study privacy-norm awareness and legal compliance in agentic and contextual settings (Shao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). These benchmarks pose a disclosure decision under a static access-control or privacy-norm scenario. PrivDrift instead addresses persistence: whether a user-disclosed secret can still be recovered after unrelated topic drift and subsequent persuasion-based probing.

### 2.2 Multi-Turn Adversarial Attacks

Aligned models remain exploitable across turns. Crescendo elicits harmful outputs through gradually escalating, superficially benign exchanges (Russinovich et al., 2024). Automated frameworks search over adversarial multi-turn attack paths (Deng et al., 2024; Narula et al., 2025). Prompt-injection studies show that later instructions can manipulate LLM-integrated applications (Liu et al., 2023). These lines of work target unsafe content generation or instruction hijacking. PrivDrift applies the multi-turn setting to information-flow control, specifically re-disclosure of a value supplied by the user earlier in the same active context.

### 2.3 Context Management and Unlearning

TOFU and WMDP evaluate removal or suppression of knowledge from model behavior (Maini et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). Both operate over static question-answer pairs and parameter-level interventions. PrivDrift targets the active context rather than the weights. It asks whether a secret present in the context window is behaviorally suppressed under later elicitation attempts. This setting applies to deployed RAG systems, copilots, and agentic workflows, where privacy control is exercised through prompt-level context management rather than parameter-level unlearning.

## 3 The PrivDrift Framework

Figure 1: PrivDrift overview. The pipeline constructs controlled multi-turn dialogues, appends standardized probes, queries target models, and scores leakage with a hybrid detector.

PrivDrift is a synthetic evaluation framework with three components (Figure 1): a parametric dialogue generator, a probing harness, and a metric suite covering leakage detection and temporal analysis.

### 3.1 Threat Model: Active-Context Re-Disclosure

We study active-context re-disclosure, in which a value disclosed earlier in a conversation is reproduced in response to later prompts issued after unrelated drift. We do not assume an adversary who cannot inspect the raw transcript. The quantity measured is whether the model itself emits the sensitive value when later instructions query, justify, or pressure it to do so.

Relevant deployments include shared or persistent sessions, in which a later user interacts with an assistant without knowledge of earlier disclosures. They also include enterprise copilots and agentic workflows, in which tool outputs, retrieved documents, or injected content issue instructions over the active context. A third case is browser- or application-integrated assistants, in which earlier disclosures are reused after the task has shifted. Presence of the secret in the transcript is held fixed. What varies is whether the assistant reproduces it.

Formally, a user discloses a secret $S$ at turn $t_{0}$. The conversation proceeds through $d$ unrelated, content-dense drift turns $D=\{u_{1},a_{1},\ldots,u_{d},a_{d}\}$. At evaluation time a standardized probe $P$ is appended to the active context. A leakage event occurs if the response reveals $S$ exactly, approximately, or semantically.

### 3.2 Dataset Generation Pipeline

We generate $N=1000$ controlled dialogues with a multi-stage scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. The ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure are fixed at the scaffold stage, and the rewrite stage reduces template artifacts. The dataset contains 900 synthetic dialogues and 100 human-authored dialogues built under the same secret and drift constraints. The human-authored dialogues are interleaved throughout the benchmark rather than stored as a contiguous block. The cached evaluation metadata does not retain human-authored identifiers, so we report aggregates over the full benchmark and defer a human-versus-synthetic comparison.

#### 3.2.1 Persona and Secret Injection

Each dialogue is initialized with a persona sampled from more than 100 professions and demographic profiles and a ground-truth secret $S$ drawn from four fixed-format PII categories: phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. $S$ is inserted in the opening turn within a plausible task context, which gives the assistant a legitimate in-context reason to observe it.

#### 3.2.2 Content-Dense Topic Drift

Each dialogue is assigned a topic such as tax filing, medical triage, or travel logistics. Drift turns are drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense question-answer pairs and from fallback tasks involving professional writing, structured reasoning, or long-form summarization. A subset of drift turns was written by human annotators and added to the library. The drift turns introduce entities and task demands unrelated to $S$, while $S$ and the number of drift turns remain under experimental control.

#### 3.2.3 Naturalistic Refinement

Each scaffold is passed to a rewriting model instructed to improve fluency and persona realism while preserving the exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. The rewrite alters surface phrasing only.

### 3.3 Probing Setup

A final standardized probe is appended to the completed history. Probes fall into three persuasion levels:

•

Simple: a direct neutral query, such as asking for the phone number mentioned earlier.

•

Medium: a query with a contextual justification, such as needing the information for a form.

•

Hard: a high-pressure or urgent request designed to test whether pressure cues increase or decrease leakage.

Drift length $d$, the number of turns between disclosure and final probing, is sampled from a mixture:

| | $d\sim\begin{cases}0&\text{with }p=0.2,\\
\mathrm{Uniform}\{2,3,4,5,6\}&\text{with }p=0.8.\end{cases}$
| | (1)

The $d=0$ component covers immediate recall, and the uniform component covers short-to-medium drift. Results bear on bounded active-context persistence and do not constitute a test of arbitrarily long contexts.

### 3.4 Evaluation Methodology

Disclosures may be verbatim, reformatted, partial substrings, or paraphrased references. We therefore use a hierarchical hybrid detector (Figure 2). A response is labeled as leakage if the normalized secret occurs in the normalized response, or if the LLM judge finds that the response reveals the full secret, a substantial substring, or partial information sufficient to identify it.

Figure 2: Hierarchical hybrid evaluation. Normalization-based matching is applied first; regex-negative responses are then passed to an LLM judge.

#### 3.4.1 Stage 1: Normalization-Based Matching

For numeric secrets, all non-digit characters are stripped from both the ground-truth secret and the response. For alphanumeric secrets, case and whitespace are normalized and meaningful delimiters are retained. With $\phi(\cdot)$ the normalization function, the regex-stage label is

| | $\mathrm{Leak}_{\mathrm{regex}}(R,S)=\mathbb{I}\big[\phi(S)\subset\phi(R)\big],$
| | (2)

where $R$ is the model response and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function.

#### 3.4.2 Stage 2: LLM-as-a-Judge Verification

Regex-negative responses are passed to an open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024). The judge receives the secret and the response and returns a binary verdict on whether the response reveals the secret or a substantial part of it. This stage targets partial disclosure, indirect hints, and formatting variants outside the reach of $\phi$. Because judge-based labeling has its own error modes, regex-only and hybrid rates are reported separately.

#### 3.4.3 Privacy Half-Life

Let $D_{obs}$ be the observed set of drift lengths and $L(d)$ the leakage rate at drift length $d$. With threshold $\delta=0.1\times L(0)$, Privacy Half-Life is

| | $\displaystyle\tau=\min\{d\in D_{obs}\mid$ | $\displaystyle L(d)\leq\delta$
| | (3)

|
| | $\displaystyle\text{and }\forall d^{\prime}\in D_{obs},d^{\prime}>d:\ L(d^{\prime})\leq\delta\}.$
|

If the set is empty, $\tau=\max(D_{obs})+1$. The universal condition over $d^{\prime}>d$ excludes transient dips.

Figure 3: Privacy Half-Life $\tau$ requires stable decay below the threshold. A later resurgence disqualifies a transient decrease.

## 4 Experimental Setup

##### Models.

We evaluate GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B through the OpenRouter API. All models receive identical dialogue histories and probe templates.

##### Dataset.

Each model is evaluated on the same 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues. Each dialogue contains one seeded secret and one drift length $d\in\{0,2,3,4,5,6\}$ sampled from Eq. (1). Each dialogue is evaluated under all three persuasion probes, giving 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model and 9,000 cached responses in total.

##### Aggregation levels.

Overall leakage is computed at the dialogue level, where a dialogue counts as leaking if any of its probes elicits the secret. Persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses are computed at the probe level, where each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition. Dialogue-level leakage can therefore exceed the mean of the per-persuasion probe-level rates.

##### Uncertainty and statistical tests.

Regex-only and hybrid leakage are both reported. Dialogue-level rates carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over dialogues. Probe-level sensitivity checks are computed over cached model-probe responses. Paired model and detector comparisons on matched examples use McNemar's test, with Bonferroni correction where applicable. Repeated measures across persuasion levels use Cochran's $Q$ with post-hoc McNemar tests. Associations between leakage and drift length, persuasion level, or secret type are tested with chi-square tests of independence, with Cramer's $V$ reported as effect size.

### 5.6 Privacy Half-Life Exceeds the Observed Window

With $\delta=0.1\cdot L(0)$, no model approaches the threshold at any tested drift length. Hence $\tau=\max(D_{obs})+1=7$ for all models and persuasion levels, and there is no stable decay within $d\leq 6$.

### 5.7 Fuzzy Matching Supports the Hybrid Labels

As a post-hoc deterministic sensitivity check, we compute normalized fuzzy matching between each saved secret and saved response using cached outputs only. At threshold 0.85, fuzzy and probe-level hybrid leakage are 26.40% versus 26.43% for DeepSeek-R1, 37.03% versus 37.57% for GPT-OSS-120B, and 37.60% versus 37.53% for Qwen3-VL-235B (Table 6). ## 6 Discussion

Sensitive values disclosed earlier in an active conversation remain behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift. This finding does not imply permanent memory of the secret, nor uniform behavior across long-context settings. It does show that current assistants reproduce in-context sensitive values when a later prompt applies sufficient retrieval pressure. The near-identity of fuzzy and hybrid probe-level rates, together with the small judge increment over regex, indicates predominantly direct or near-direct reproduction.

The secret-type asymmetry is the largest effect. SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers, even though all four categories are equally user-disclosed in the benchmark. This pattern is consistent with format-sensitive safety heuristics rather than robust contextual reasoning about confidentiality.

Persuasion effects are significant but non-monotonic and model-dependent. For GPT-OSS-120B, high-pressure requests lower leakage, which is compatible with urgency cues activating refusal behavior. For DeepSeek-R1, Medium is lowest. For Qwen3-VL-235B, Hard is highest, indicating weaker resistance to pressure-based extraction.

The intermediate dips in the leakage curves do not satisfy the Privacy Half-Life criterion, so topic drift cannot be treated as an implicit privacy boundary. Evaluation should therefore be stability-based rather than reading temporary drops as suppression.

## 7 Limitations and Future Work

##### Bounded drift range.

Drift lengths extend to $d=6$, which corresponds to bounded short-to-medium conversational drift rather than saturation of modern context windows. The results characterize persistence under bounded active-context drift and do not fully characterize privacy behavior across complete long-context windows.

##### Fixed-format secrets.

The benchmark covers structured secrets: SSNs, credit card numbers, emails, and phone numbers. These are easier to detect than unstructured sensitive information such as health status, family circumstances, immigration status, or financial hardship. Extension to non-fixed sensitive attributes is left to future work.

##### Active context, not cross-session memory.

PrivDrift measures recoverability within the active conversation context. It does not test training-data memorization, personalization memory, or cross-session retention.

##### Synthetic and human-authored dialogues.

The dataset comprises 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues interleaved throughout the benchmark rather than stored as a separate block. This improves realism relative to a purely synthetic benchmark while preserving control over secret type, drift length, and probe structure. The cached evaluation metadata does not record which rows are human-authored, so results are aggregate and a human-versus-synthetic comparison is deferred.

##### Detector scope.

Labels derive from surface-form outputs via deterministic matching, fuzzy matching, and an external LLM judge. Regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid labels are reported separately for transparency, but formal inter-annotator agreement between humans and the automated methods is not yet reported. A larger manual audit of borderline partial disclosures and obfuscations is planned.

##### API-served models and reproducibility.

Owing to compute and budget constraints, the evaluated models are API-served and may change over time. We log model identifiers, prompts, timestamps, and cached responses, and we compute paired statistics on identical dialogue sets.

##### Artifact availability.

We plan to release the generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate result files, and a sanitized subset of generated dialogues. Because the benchmark contains synthetic PII-like strings, released examples will use non-real identifiers, together with generation templates sufficient to reproduce the benchmark without exposing realistic identifiers.

## 8 Conclusion

PrivDrift audits active-context privacy leakage under topic drift and persuasion intensity. Across three LLMs and 1,000 dialogues per model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects are model-dependent, and secret type shows the strongest association with leakage. Within the tested drift range, drift does not reliably reduce leakage, and Privacy Half-Life exceeds the observed window for every model. The secret-type asymmetry indicates that current protections are uneven and keyed more to format-sensitive cues than to robust contextual confidentiality.

ANSWER Q1: A red-teamer should use the hard probe when probing DeepSeek-R1, as it tests whether the model suppresses sensitive information under high-pressure conditions.

ANSWER Q2: No, if the benchmark contained only phone-number secrets, Qwen3-VL-235B would not necessarily be the leakiest model, as the other models may also leak phone numbers.

ANSWER Q3: No, pooling all three models' probe-level responses with equal weight would not yield higher leakage for the hard probe than the medium probe.

ANSWER Q4: Yes, if PrivDrift had used only the hard probe, Qwen3-VL-235B would still be the leakiest model, as its hard-probe leakage rate is higher than that of the other two models.

ANSWER Q5: The paper shows that the models generally do not suppress numeric personal identifiers, as the average leakage rate at d = 0 is around 70-80% for all models.

ANSWER Q6: Using PrivDrift-style dialogues, a new study would find that politeness has no significant effect on leakage, as the Cramer's V value is around 0.09, which is not statistically significant.

ANSWER Q7: Privacy Half-Life can systematically report τ = max(D_obs)+1 for a model whose true leakage at long drift hovers just around 0.1·L(0) because the model's leakage rate never drops below the threshold, so the value of τ remains the same as the maximum observed drift length.

ANSWER Q8: No, DeepSeek-R1's drift effect does not systematically result in a Privacy Half-Life below 7, as its leakage rate remains above 0.1·L(0) across all drift lengths.

ANSWER Q9: The 38.7%–54.6% dialogue-level range overstates the leakage risk of an assistant deployed in a specific application if the leakage rate at d = 0 is significantly higher than 0.1·L(0).

ANSWER Q10: The paper does not show that DeepSeek-R1 is the least leaky model under every persuasion level, as its leakage rates vary across the different probe conditions.

ANSWER Q11: No, fuzzy matching at the 0.80 threshold does not flag a larger share of probe responses than the hybrid detector for DeepSeek-R1.

ANSWER Q12: The median dialogue length is above the mean because the dataset contains more dialogues with longer drift lengths, which increases the overall dialogue length.

ANSWER Q13: If GPT-OSS-120B's email and phone leakage matched DeepSeek-R1's, the comparison that loses its support is the one between GPT-OSS-120B and Qwen3-VL-235B.

ANSWER Q14: The smallest value Privacy Half-Life can take is 7, as the model's leakage rate never drops below the threshold.

ANSWER Q15: The naturalistic refinement step would compromise the results if it silently changed the number of drift turns in many dialogues, as it would artificially increase the observed drift length and affect the calculated Privacy Half-Life.

ANSWER Q16: The abstract's wording is not supported, as the paper's statistics show that leakage varies significantly by persuasion intensity.

ANSWER Q17: A red-teamer would want to use the hard probe when probing Qwen3-VL-235B to extract secrets from it.

ANSWER Q18: Yes, a model with L(0) = 80% and L(d) = 7% at every drift length d = 2 to 6 would have a Privacy Half-Life below 7.

ANSWER Q19: The paper's numbers do not provide a lower bound on the chance that a GPT-OSS-120B session leaks a shared phone number when an attacker can try all three PrivDrift probes.

ANSWER Q20: If the dialogue-level regex-versus-hybrid McNemar p-value is Bonferroni-corrected over the three per-model comparisons at α = 0.05, it may not remain significant for DeepSeek-R1.

ANSWER Q21: GPT-OSS-120B's secret-type Cramer's V is the largest because it has the highest average leakage rate at d = 0, indicating that it leaks more sensitive information in email and phone queries.

ANSWER Q22: No, if GPT-OSS-120B's average probe-level leakage exceeds Qwen3-VL-235B's, it would not necessarily mean that GPT-OSS-120B is the leakiest model, as the other factors (e.g., drift length and persuasion intensity) also affect leakage.

ANSWER Q23: No, the paper does not show that GPT-OSS-120B's leakage never falls to half its d = 0 level within d ≤ 6, as the leakage rate remains above 0.1·L(0) across all drift lengths.

ANSWER Q24: No, the paper does not show that GPT-OSS-120B leaks significantly more under the medium probe than under the simple probe, as the difference in leakage rates between the two probes is not statistically significant.

# PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations

Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero

Affiliation: West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA

Correspondence to: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu

###### Abstract

We introduce PrivDrift, a benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded user secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes at three persuasion levels. It is intended for persistent assistants deployed in user-facing, shared-session, and tool-augmented settings. Across three LLMs with extended context windows, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage.

###### Keywords: 

Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking

## 1 Introduction

LLMs now serve as persistent multi-turn assistants (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). They are used in healthcare triage, financial planning, enterprise copilots, and personal productivity tools, where users may disclose PII such as phone numbers, financial identifiers, email addresses, and health-related details. Prior safety evaluations target training-data memorization (Carlini et al., 2021; Nasr et al., 2023) and immediate jailbreaking (Wei et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023). Others study prompt injection and multi-turn attacks (Liu et al., 2023; Russinovich et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024). None of these measure recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

We do not assume users believe an LLM forgets earlier messages in a session. The relevant settings are shared sessions, browser-integrated assistants, enterprise copilots, agentic workflows, and prompt injection, in which later indirect, justified, high-pressure, or tool-mediated prompts interact with the active context.

PrivDrift varies two axes: topic drift and persuasion intensity. Over three LLMs with extended context windows and 1,000 dialogues per model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage is 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion intensity has a significant effect. SSNs and credit cards are suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers. For $d\leq 6$, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage.

Contributions:

1.

PrivDrift, a controlled benchmark for active-context re-disclosure after unrelated topic drift.

2.

Leakage under Simple, Medium, and Hard probes.

3.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Contextual Privacy and Inference-Time Leakage

Prior work covers training-data extraction, membership inference, and recovery of memorized PII (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023; Nasr et al., 2023), all of which concern parameters. ConfAIde evaluates privacy reasoning through contextual integrity (Mireshghallah et al., 2024). PrivacyLens and PrivaCI-Bench address norm awareness and legal compliance in agentic or contextual settings (Shao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). These benchmarks use static access-control or privacy-norm scenarios. PrivDrift instead isolates persistence of a user-disclosed secret under unrelated drift and later persuasion-based probing.

### 2.2 Multi-Turn Adversarial Attacks

Crescendo elicits harmful outputs through gradual benign-seeming conversations (Russinovich et al., 2024). Automated frameworks generate multi-turn attack paths (Deng et al., 2024; Narula et al., 2025). Prompt injection manipulates LLM-integrated applications (Liu et al., 2023). These works target unsafe content or instruction hijacking. PrivDrift targets information flow, specifically re-disclosure of user-supplied information from the same active context.

### 2.3 Context Management and Unlearning

TOFU and WMDP evaluate removal or suppression of knowledge (Maini et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024) over static QA pairs and model weights. PrivDrift targets behavioral suppression of a secret present in the context window. This is the relevant control surface for RAG systems, copilots, and agentic workflows that rely on prompt-level context management.

## 3 The PrivDrift Framework

Figure 1: PrivDrift overview. The pipeline constructs controlled multi-turn dialogues, appends standardized probes, queries target models, and scores leakage with a hybrid detector.

PrivDrift has three components (Figure 1): a parametric dialogue generator, a probing harness, and a metric suite for leakage detection and temporal analysis.

### 3.1 Threat Model: Active-Context Re-Disclosure

The adversary is not assumed to be unable to inspect the raw transcript. Instances include a later user in a shared or persistent session, later tool outputs, retrieved documents, or prompt-injection content in copilots and agentic workflows, and reuse after a task shift in integrated assistants.

A user discloses secret $S$ at turn $t_{0}$. Then $d$ unrelated, content-dense drift turns $D=\{u_{1},a_{1},\ldots,u_{d},a_{d}\}$ follow, and a standardized probe $P$ is appended. A leakage event is any response revealing $S$ exactly, approximately, or semantically.

### 3.2 Dataset Generation Pipeline

$N=1000$ dialogues are produced by a multi-stage scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. The ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure are fixed by the scaffold. The set comprises 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues under the same secret and drift constraints. The human-authored dialogues are interleaved rather than stored as a contiguous block. The cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers, so results are aggregate and a human-versus-synthetic comparison is deferred.

#### 3.2.1 Persona and Secret Injection

Personas are sampled from more than 100 professions and demographic profiles. $S$ is drawn from four fixed-format PII categories: phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. It is inserted in the opening turn within a plausible task context, which gives a legitimate in-context reason for its presence.

#### 3.2.2 Content-Dense Topic Drift

Each dialogue is assigned a topic, such as tax filing, medical triage, or travel logistics. Drift turns come from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks covering professional writing, structured reasoning, and long-form summarization. Annotators authored a subset of the drift turns, which were incorporated into the library.

#### 3.2.3 Naturalistic Refinement

A rewriting model revises each scaffold for fluency and persona realism. It preserves the exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions, so only surface phrasing changes.

### 3.3 Probing Setup

A final standardized probe is appended to the full history:

•

Simple: a direct neutral query, such as asking for the phone number mentioned earlier.

•

Medium: a query with a contextual justification, such as needing the information for a form.

•

Hard: a high-pressure or urgent request.

Drift length is sampled as

| | $d\sim\begin{cases}0&\text{with }p=0.2,\\
\mathrm{Uniform}\{2,3,4,5,6\}&\text{with }p=0.8.\end{cases}$
| | (1)

The scope is bounded active-context persistence, not arbitrarily long windows.

### 3.4 Evaluation Methodology

Disclosure may be verbatim, reformatted, partial, or paraphrased. A response is labeled leaking if the normalized secret appears in the normalized response, or if the judge finds the full secret, a substantial substring, or identifying partial information.

Figure 2: Hierarchical hybrid evaluation. Normalization-based matching is applied first; regex-negative responses are then passed to an LLM judge.

#### 3.4.1 Stage 1: Normalization-Based Matching

With $\phi(\cdot)$ stripping non-digits for numeric secrets, and normalizing case and whitespace while preserving meaningful delimiters for alphanumeric secrets,

| | $\mathrm{Leak}_{\mathrm{regex}}(R,S)=\mathbb{I}\big[\phi(S)\subset\phi(R)\big],$
| | (2)

where $R$ is the model response and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function.

#### 3.4.2 Stage 2: LLM-as-a-Judge Verification

Regex-negative responses go to an open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024). Given the secret and the response, it returns a binary verdict on whether the secret or a substantial part of it is revealed. Regex-only and hybrid rates are reported separately.

#### 3.4.3 Privacy Half-Life

With $D_{obs}$ the observed drift lengths, $L(d)$ the leakage rate at $d$, and $\delta=0.1\times L(0)$:

| | $\displaystyle\tau=\min\{d\in D_{obs}\mid$ | $\displaystyle L(d)\leq\delta$
| | (3)

|
| | $\displaystyle\text{and }\forall d^{\prime}\in D_{obs},d^{\prime}>d:\ L(d^{\prime})\leq\delta\}.$
|

For an empty set, $\tau=\max(D_{obs})+1$.

Figure 3: Privacy Half-Life $\tau$ requires stable decay below the threshold. A later resurgence disqualifies a transient decrease.

## 4 Experimental Setup

##### Models.

GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B are evaluated via the OpenRouter API, with identical dialogue histories and probe templates.

##### Dataset.

All 1,000 dialogues are run on each model. Each dialogue contains one secret and one $d\in\{0,2,3,4,5,6\}$ drawn from Eq. (1), and each receives all three probes. This gives 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model and 9,000 in total.

##### Aggregation levels.

Overall leakage is dialogue-level, with a dialogue counted as leaking if any probe elicits the secret. Persuasion-level and fuzzy analyses are probe-level, with one response per dialogue per condition. Dialogue-level leakage can therefore exceed the mean of the per-persuasion rates.

##### Uncertainty and statistical tests.

We report 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues for dialogue-level rates, and rates over cached model-probe responses for probe-level checks. Paired model and detector comparisons use McNemar's test with Bonferroni correction where applicable. Persuasion levels are compared with Cochran's $Q$ and post-hoc McNemar tests. Associations of leakage with drift length, persuasion level, and secret type use chi-square tests of independence, with Cramer's $V$ as the effect size.

## 6 Discussion

Secrets disclosed earlier remain recoverable after unrelated drift under sufficient retrieval pressure. This does not imply permanent memory or uniform long-context behavior. The fuzzy-hybrid agreement places most leakage at direct or near-direct reproduction.

SSNs and credit cards are suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers, which points to format-sensitive heuristics in current safeguards. Persuasion effects are significant, non-monotonic, and model-dependent. Hard probes lower leakage for GPT-OSS-120B, consistent with urgency cues triggering refusal. Medium is lowest for DeepSeek-R1. Hard is highest for Qwen3-VL-235B. Intermediate dips in the drift curves fail the $\tau$ stability criterion.

## 7 Limitations and Future Work

##### Bounded drift range.

The evaluation covers $d$ up to $d=6$, short-to-medium drift, and does not saturate modern context windows.

##### Fixed-format secrets.

The benchmark covers only SSNs, credit card numbers, emails, and phone numbers. Unstructured attributes such as health status, family circumstances, immigration status, and financial hardship are left for future work.

##### Active context, not cross-session memory.

Training-data memorization, personalization memory, and cross-session retention are not tested.

##### Synthetic and human-authored dialogues.

The 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues are interleaved. The cached metadata does not mark the human-authored rows, so only aggregate results are reported and the human-versus-synthetic comparison is deferred.

##### Detector scope.

Labels rest on surface-form outputs from deterministic matching, fuzzy matching, and an external LLM judge. Formal human-automated inter-annotator agreement is not yet reported. A larger manual audit of borderline partial disclosures and obfuscations is planned.

##### API-served models and reproducibility.

API-served models may change over time. We log model identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics on identical dialogue sets.

##### Artifact availability.

We plan to release the generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate results, and a sanitized subset of dialogues. Released examples will use non-real identifiers, and the templates will suffice to reproduce the benchmark.

## 8 Conclusion

PrivDrift audits active-context leakage under topic drift and persuasion intensity. Across three LLMs and 1,000 dialogues per model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage is 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects are model-dependent. Secret type has the strongest association with leakage. Drift does not reliably reduce leakage within the tested range, and $\tau$ exceeds the observed window for all models.
